1 Timothy 1.summary: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and Christ Jesus our hope, writes to Timothy, whom he calls his true child in the faith, with a greeting of grace, mercy and peace (1 Timothy 1:1-2). He reminds Timothy that he urged him, when he was going to Macedonia, to remain at Ephesus so that he might charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith (1 Timothy 1:3-4). The aim of the charge is love that issues from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith, but some have swerved from these and wandered into vain discussion, wanting to be teachers of the law without understanding what they say (1 Timothy 1:5-7). Paul says the law is good if used lawfully; it is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, and for whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God entrusted to him (1 Timothy 1:8-11). He thanks Christ Jesus for strengthening him and appointing him to service, though he was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent who received mercy because he acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:12-14). He gives a trustworthy saying: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom Paul says he is the foremost, and he received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15-16). A doxology to the King of the ages follows (1 Timothy 1:17). Paul then entrusts the charge to Timothy in line with earlier prophecies about him, so that he may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and made shipwreck of their faith, among them Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:18-20).
1 Timothy 1.whereWeAre:
Paul had worked in Ephesus for about two to three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31), and told the Ephesian elders that people would arise from among them speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29-30).

Ephesus had a large Jewish community and the famous temple of Artemis (Acts 19:27, 19:35). Jewish teaching, local religion and Greek ideas were all present; the letter does not say which shaped the false teaching.

Timothy joined Paul on his second journey, after Paul met him at Lystra (Acts 16:1-3), and he is mentioned as a co-worker in several letters.

Genealogies were important in Jewish and Greek traditions to establish identity and origins, but the letter does not say which genealogies are meant.

Early Christian tradition (for example Eusebius, Church History 3.4.5) says that Timothy was the first bishop of Ephesus. This is a later tradition and not stated in the letter. The letter's opening shows a church in Ephesus facing teachers who were drawing people away from the gospel. Timothy's task is to confront them without losing sight of the aim of love, and Paul's own story gives a model of the mercy that sound teaching is meant to protect.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Writes to Timothy, gives the charge, tells his own story of mercy, and hands Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan. His life illustrates the gospel of grace and gives authority to the charge.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Left at Ephesus to charge certain people; given the charge to wage the good warfare. The recipient of the letter and the one responsible for its instructions.

keyFigures.name: Certain persons who teach different doctrine
keyFigures.role: Said to teach different doctrine, devote themselves to myths and genealogies, and desire to be teachers of the law without understanding it. Their activity is the reason Timothy is at Ephesus.

keyFigures.name: Hymenaeus and Alexander
keyFigures.role: Paul handed them over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme. Their example is a warning. A Hymenaeus appears also in 2 Timothy 2:17 and an Alexander in 2 Timothy 4:14; whether they are the same men is not stated.

keyFigures.name: God and Christ Jesus
keyFigures.role: Commands Paul's apostleship, strengthens and appoints Paul, and shows mercy and patience. The gospel and Paul's calling rest on their action.

keyFigures.name: Macedonia and Ephesus (places)
keyFigures.role: Mentioned as the places where Paul was going and where Timothy is to stay. They show Paul's travel and Timothy's assignment.

keyThemes.theme: Sound teaching and the aim of love
keyThemes.explanation:
The charge aims at love from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith, and false teaching is described as a swerve from this.

The chapter invites readers to measure teaching by whether it leads to love and a sincere faith, as well as by its content.

keyThemes.theme: The right use of the law
keyThemes.explanation:
The law is good if used lawfully and is aimed at the lawless and disobedient.

Readers are invited to consider that the law has a purpose and can be misused.

keyThemes.theme: Grace and mercy toward the worst of sinners
keyThemes.explanation:
Paul describes himself as a former blasphemer and persecutor who received mercy, and gives the saying that Christ Jesus came to save sinners.

The passage encourages hope that mercy is available even for those with a bad past.

Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and appointing him to service.

The passage frames ministry as a responsibility that depends on Christ's enabling.

keyThemes.theme: Holding faith and a good conscience
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is to wage the good warfare holding faith and a good conscience, unlike those who made shipwreck of their faith.

The chapter treats faith and conscience as things to be guarded.

1 Timothy 2.summary: Paul urges that supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that believers may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way (1 Timothy 2:1-2). This is good and pleasing to God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:3-4). There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5-6). Paul was appointed a preacher, an apostle and a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth (1 Timothy 2:7). He then desires that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling (1 Timothy 2:8). Likewise women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with good works (1 Timothy 2:9-10). A woman is to learn quietly with all submissiveness; Paul says he does not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but she is to remain quiet, and he gives a reason from the creation of Adam and Eve and the deception of the woman (1 Timothy 2:11-14). He ends with the statement that she will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control (1 Timothy 2:15).
1 Timothy 2.whereWeAre:
Prayer for rulers has a background in the Old Testament, where the exiles were told to seek the welfare of the city (Jeremiah 29:7) and where the Persian king's welfare was prayed for (Ezra 6:10).

Paul elsewhere speaks of Christians living quietly and respecting authorities (Romans 13:1-7; 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12).

Wealthy women in the Greco-Roman world were known for elaborate hairstyles and costly jewelry, and moralists such as Plutarch (Advice to Bride and Groom) criticized extravagant dress. The letter does not say what prompted this instruction.

Women had varied roles in the early church, including Priscilla, who with Aquila explained the way of God more accurately to Apollos (Acts 18:26), and Phoebe, called a servant of the church (Romans 16:1). This is relevant to discussion of 2:12 but does not settle how the verse is to be read.

Some scholars connect the teaching on women in 2:9-15 to the false teaching in Ephesus or to the influence of the cult of Artemis. This is a proposed reconstruction, and the letter does not state it. The instructions on prayer, dress and women's teaching are given to a church in a specific city with a particular set of challenges. The background shows both the concern for good public witness and the difficulty of reconstructing the exact situation.

keyFigures.name: Believers (the church)
keyFigures.role: Told to pray for all people and kings, to pray without anger, and to conduct themselves in a godly way. The instructions are addressed to the community as a whole.

keyFigures.name: Kings and those in high positions
keyFigures.role: Prayed for. The prayer shows the church's relationship to the authorities.

keyFigures.name: God our Savior
keyFigures.role: Described as pleased with prayer for all and as the one God. The basis of the church's prayer and mission.

keyFigures.name: Christ Jesus
keyFigures.role: Gave himself as a ransom for all. The center of the chapter's teaching about salvation.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Describes his appointment as a preacher, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, and gives instructions. His appointment supports the universal reach of the gospel.

keyFigures.name: Men and women in the congregation
keyFigures.role: Men are told to pray without anger; women are told about dress, learning and teaching. The instructions show expectations for conduct in the assembly.

keyFigures.name: Adam and Eve
keyFigures.role: Cited as the basis for the instruction in 2:13-14. The reason shows how Paul appeals to Scripture.

keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to pray for all, including rulers, so that they may live peaceful and quiet lives.

The chapter invites readers to see prayer for others, including authorities, as a central part of the church's life.

There is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.

The passage calls readers to hold together God's desire for the salvation of all and Christ's role as the one mediator.

The aim of the prayer is a peaceful and quiet life that is godly and dignified in every way.

The chapter invites reflection on how character and conduct support the church's witness.

Men are to pray lifting holy hands, without anger or quarreling.

Readers are invited to consider how conflict affects prayer.

keyThemes.theme: Conduct and roles in the assembly
keyThemes.explanation:
Women are given instruction about adornment, learning and teaching, with reasons from creation.

Readers are encouraged to study the passage carefully, noting that Christian traditions differ on its application.

1 Timothy 3.summary: Paul gives a trustworthy saying: if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1). An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable and able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome and not a lover of money (1 Timothy 3:2-3). He must manage his own household well, keeping his children submissive with all dignity, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church 1 Timothy 3:4-5? He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil, and he must be well thought of by outsiders so that he does not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6-7). Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, and tested first (1 Timothy 3:8-10). Their wives, or women, likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, sober-minded and faithful in all things (1 Timothy 3:11). Deacons are each to be the husband of one wife, managing their children and households well, and those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in the faith (1 Timothy 3:12-13). Paul hopes to come soon but writes so that, if he delays, Timothy may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth (1 Timothy 3:14-15). He ends with the confession that great is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory (1 Timothy 3:16).
1 Timothy 3.whereWeAre:
Elders in Ephesus are mentioned in Acts 20:17, and Paul addresses them as overseers in Acts 20:28.

Paul appointed elders in churches on his journeys (Acts 14:23) and instructed Titus to appoint elders in Crete (Titus 1:5-9).

Paul addresses 'overseers and deacons' in Philippians 1:1, showing that these roles existed in other churches.

The household was the basic social unit of the ancient world, including family members, slaves, and dependents. The head of a household was expected to maintain order.

Whether the church offices were as formal as in later centuries is debated; the letter does not describe how overseers and deacons were chosen. The qualifications reflect expectations of leadership in a household-based church and the concern for the church's reputation in the surrounding society. The 'household' language ties the church's order to its identity as God's family.

keyFigures.name: Overseer (a leader in the church)
keyFigures.role: The character and household of the person are described. The qualifications reveal what the letter values in a leader.

keyFigures.name: Deacons
keyFigures.role: Must be dignified, tested and faithful in their households. Their service is said to give a good standing and great confidence in the faith.

keyFigures.name: Their wives or women
keyFigures.role: Told to be dignified, not slanderers, sober-minded and faithful. The passage shows concern for the character of all who serve.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Expresses hope to come soon and gives the purpose for writing. His instructions are given to Timothy for the church's life.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: The one who is to know how to behave in the household of God. He is the recipient of the instructions.

keyFigures.name: Outsiders
keyFigures.role: The overseer must be well thought of by them. Their view matters to the church's witness.

keyFigures.name: The devil
keyFigures.role: Associated with a condemnation and a snare. The warnings show the danger of pride and disgrace.

keyFigures.name: Christ
keyFigures.role: Manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory. The confession is the center of 'the mystery of godliness.'

keyThemes.explanation:
Qualifications for overseers and deacons focus largely on character and conduct.

The chapter invites readers to consider character as central to leadership.

An overseer must manage his own household well, as a test of caring for the church.

Readers are invited to see the connection between private life and public responsibility.

Overseers are to be well thought of by outsiders; deacons are to be tested first.

The passage encourages careful discernment before giving responsibility.

The church is described as the household of God, the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.

Believers are invited to see the church's life as the life of God's household.

keyThemes.theme: The mystery of godliness centered on Christ
keyThemes.explanation:
The confession in 3:16 sums up the mystery of godliness in lines about Christ.

The conduct described is grounded in the person and work of Christ.

1 Timothy 4.summary: Paul says the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared (1 Timothy 4:1-2). These people forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth (1 Timothy 4:3). Paul answers that everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4-5). If Timothy puts these things before the brothers, he will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine (1 Timothy 4:6). He is to have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths but to train himself for godliness; bodily training is of some value, but godliness is of value in every way, with promise for the present life and the life to come (1 Timothy 4:7-8). A trustworthy saying follows: Paul and his companions toil and strive because their hope is set on the living God, the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe (1 Timothy 4:9-10). Timothy is to command and teach these things, and not let anyone despise him for his youth, but set believers an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity (1 Timothy 4:11-12). Until Paul comes, he is to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, exhortation and teaching, and not neglect the gift that was given him by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on him (1 Timothy 4:13-14). He is to practice these things, immerse himself in them so that all may see his progress, and keep a close watch on himself and the teaching, for by this he will save both himself and his hearers (1 Timothy 4:15-16).
1 Timothy 4.whereWeAre:
Timothy served in Ephesus (1:3), and Paul had earlier warned the Ephesian elders of coming error (Acts 20:29-30).

The Old Testament and Jewish law included food laws (Leviticus 11), and Jesus declared all foods clean in Mark 7:19. The early church debated food and ritual questions (Acts 10; 15; Romans 14).

Marriage is affirmed in Scripture as part of creation (Genesis 2:24) and in Hebrews 13:4. Some ancient groups practiced celibacy or abstinence from certain foods, but the letter does not say which, if any, matches the teachers in Ephesus.

The public reading of Scripture was a central feature of Jewish synagogue worship (Luke 4:16-21; Acts 13:15) and was carried over into early Christian gatherings (compare Colossians 4:16).

Greek culture valued physical training, and gymnasiums were common in cities, including Ephesus. The letter uses this familiar image for comparison. The warnings and instructions address a church facing teaching that restricted what God had made good. The references to Scripture reading and example show how the early church sought to maintain sound teaching.

keyFigures.name: The Spirit
keyFigures.role: Warns of departure from the faith. The warning has divine authority in the letter.

keyFigures.name: Teachers of error / liars
keyFigures.role: Described as insincere, with seared consciences, devoted to deceitful spirits. They represent the danger Timothy must address.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Told to teach, to avoid myths, to set an example, and to devote himself to Scripture, exhortation and teaching. The chapter's instructions apply to his ministry.

keyFigures.name: Paul and his companions
keyFigures.role: Say that they toil and strive because their hope is set on the living God. Their example supports the instruction to Timothy.

keyFigures.name: The brothers
keyFigures.role: Recipients of Timothy's teaching. The community is the audience of the instruction.

keyFigures.name: The council of elders
keyFigures.role: Associated with the gift given to Timothy by prophecy. They connect Timothy's ministry to the community.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Created everything good and is the hope of Paul and his companions. The basis for the chapter's teaching on creation and hope.

keyFigures.name: Christ Jesus
keyFigures.role: Timothy will be a good servant of Christ Jesus. The standard of Timothy's service.

keyThemes.explanation:
Everything created by God is good and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving.

The passage invites readers to receive God's gifts with thanksgiving.

The Spirit warns that some will depart from the faith and follow deceitful teaching.

The chapter encourages awareness of teaching that departs from the faith.

Godliness is compared to bodily training and said to be of value in every way.

Readers are invited to give attention to spiritual growth.

Timothy is to set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, despite his youth.

The passage encourages believers of any age to live as examples.

keyThemes.theme: Devotion to Scripture, teaching and the gift
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, exhortation and teaching, and not neglect his gift.

The passage encourages sustained attention to Scripture and teaching.

1 Timothy 5.summary: Paul tells Timothy not to rebuke an older man but to encourage him as a father, to treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:1-2). The church is to honor widows who are truly widows; if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to show godliness to their own household and make a return to their parents (1 Timothy 5:3-4). A widow who is truly alone has set her hope on God and continues in prayer, while one who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives (1 Timothy 5:5-6). Anyone who does not provide for his relatives, especially his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). A widow may be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, was the wife of one husband, and has a reputation for good works (1 Timothy 5:9-10). Younger widows are not to be enrolled, and Paul would have them marry, bear children and manage their households, to give the adversary no occasion for slander (1 Timothy 5:11-15). A believing woman with widowed relatives is to care for them so that the church is not burdened and can care for those truly widows (1 Timothy 5:16). Elders who rule well are worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching, citing 'You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain' and 'The laborer deserves his wages' (1 Timothy 5:17-18). A charge against an elder is not to be admitted except on the evidence of two or three witnesses, and those who persist in sin are to be rebuked before all (1 Timothy 5:19-20). Timothy is charged in the presence of God, Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality, not to be hasty in the laying on of hands, and to keep himself pure (1 Timothy 5:21-22). Paul advises him to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23). Finally, he observes that the sins of some are conspicuous and the sins of others appear later; so also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden (1 Timothy 5:24-25).
1 Timothy 5.whereWeAre:
The Old Testament commands care for widows and the vulnerable (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 24:19-21; 27:19).

The early church in Jerusalem arranged a daily distribution that included widows (Acts 6:1).

James 1:27 describes caring for orphans and widows in their affliction as part of pure religion.

In the ancient Mediterranean world, adult children were generally expected to support aged parents, and Roman marriage legislation under Augustus encouraged widows of childbearing age to remarry.

Elders are mentioned in the churches in Ephesus (Acts 20:17), and the charge requiring two or three witnesses echoes Deuteronomy 19:15. The instructions about widows and elders reflect the real needs of a church functioning without public support systems, and they draw on Old Testament principles. The warnings reflect concern for the church's reputation and unity.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Instructed about how to treat different groups, how to handle charges against elders, and how to guard his own purity and health. He is the one who applies the instructions.

keyFigures.name: Older men, younger men, older women, younger women
keyFigures.role: Timothy is to treat them as fathers, brothers, mothers and sisters. The family language shapes how Timothy relates to all.

keyFigures.name: Widows who are truly widows
keyFigures.role: The church is to honor them; they continue in prayer. They are the primary object of the church's care.

keyFigures.name: Children and grandchildren of widows
keyFigures.role: They are to care for their own household and make a return to their parents. The family has primary responsibility.

keyFigures.name: Enrolled widows
keyFigures.role: They are to be sixty or older, wives of one husband, with a reputation for good works. Their character is the criterion for being enrolled.

keyFigures.name: Younger widows
keyFigures.role: They are not to be enrolled and are encouraged to marry. Paul expresses concern about their situation.

keyFigures.name: Elders
keyFigures.role: Elders who rule well are worthy of double honor; charges against them require two or three witnesses. Their leadership is honored and protected.

keyFigures.name: God, Christ Jesus and the elect angels
keyFigures.role: Timothy is charged before them. The charge is made solemn.

keyFigures.name: The adversary; Satan
keyFigures.role: Younger widows are to give the adversary no occasion for slander; some have already strayed after Satan. Shows the spiritual stakes of conduct.

keyThemes.theme: Honor and care for the vulnerable
keyThemes.explanation:
The church is to honor and support widows who are truly alone and families are to care for their own.

The chapter invites readers to consider both family and church responsibility for those in need.

Those who do not provide for relatives, especially household members, are said to have denied the faith.

The passage encourages readers to see care for family as an expression of faith.

Timothy is to relate to older and younger people as family members, in all purity.

The chapter invites readers to approach others with respect and purity.

Elders who rule well are worthy of double honor, and charges against them require two or three witnesses, though persistent sinners are rebuked.

Readers are invited to consider both honor and accountability in leadership.

Timothy is to keep the rules without partiality, not be hasty in the laying on of hands, and keep himself pure.

The passage encourages careful, fair, and patient judgment.

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the instruction not to muzzle a working ox.

1 Timothy 6.summary: Paul says those who are under a yoke as bondservants should regard their masters as worthy of all honor so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled; those with believing masters must not be disrespectful because they are brothers, but serve all the better (1 Timothy 6:1-2). Anyone who teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of the Lord Jesus Christ is puffed up with conceit, with an unhealthy craving for controversy and quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions and constant friction, among people who imagine that godliness is a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:3-5). But godliness with contentment is great gain: we brought nothing into the world and cannot take anything out, and if we have food and clothing, we will be content (1 Timothy 6:6-8). Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and many harmful desires, and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils; some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs (1 Timothy 6:9-10). Timothy, the man of God, is to flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness and gentleness; to fight the good fight of the faith and take hold of eternal life to which he was called (1 Timothy 6:11-12). Paul charges him, in the presence of God and Christ Jesus, who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment unstained until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Timothy 6:13-14), which God will display at the proper time; he is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light (1 Timothy 6:15-16). The rich in this age are to be charged not to be haughty nor set their hopes on riches but on God, to do good, be rich in good works, be generous and ready to share, storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:17-19). The letter ends with Timothy being told to guard the deposit entrusted to him and avoid irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called 'knowledge,' which some have professed and swerved from the faith (1 Timothy 6:20-21).
1 Timothy 6.whereWeAre:
Slavery was common in the Roman Empire, and slaves were part of many households. Some slaves belonged to Christian masters (6:2).

Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea from about AD 26 to 36. His role in Jesus' trial is recorded in the Gospels, and the Roman historian Tacitus also mentions that Christ was executed under Pilate, whom he calls a procurator (Annals 15.44).

Ephesus was a leading city of the Roman province of Asia and a major center of trade, so wealth and its temptations were present in the community addressed.

The 'false knowledge' (gnosis) could refer to various speculative teachings; the fully developed Gnostic systems are known mainly from the second century and later.

Early churches included people of differing social standing, such as Philemon and his slave Onesimus (Philemon), though (1 Corinthians 1:26-29) says that not many were of high status. The instructions about slaves, riches and false teaching reflect the church's social mix and the pressures it faced. The closing charge ties the letter's concerns to the person and testimony of Christ.

keyFigures.name: Bondservants (slaves)
keyFigures.role: Told to honor their masters and, if their masters are believers, to serve all the better. The instruction concerns the reputation of God's name and the teaching.

keyFigures.name: Believing masters
keyFigures.role: Their bondservants are not to be disrespectful because they are brothers. Shows that shared faith did not remove the existing social roles in this passage.

keyFigures.name: The teacher of different doctrine
keyFigures.role: Described as conceited, craving controversy, and imagining godliness is a means of gain. The description contrasts false teaching with godliness and contentment.

keyFigures.name: Those who desire to be rich
keyFigures.role: They fall into temptation, a snare and harmful desires. Their example shows the danger of the love of money.

keyFigures.name: Timothy (the man of God)
keyFigures.role: Told to flee these things, pursue godliness, fight the good fight and guard the deposit. The recipient of the charge.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ and Pontius Pilate
keyFigures.role: Christ's testimony is the model for the charge. Pilate is named only to identify the event of Christ's testimony; he appears as a historical reference.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives life to all things, dwells in unapproachable light. The source of the charge and the object of hope.

keyFigures.name: The rich in this present age
keyFigures.role: Charged not to be haughty or to trust in riches, but to be generous. They are given specific instruction.

keyThemes.explanation:
Godliness with contentment is called great gain, in contrast to using godliness as a means of gain.

The chapter invites readers to reflect on contentment and what truly matters.

keyThemes.theme: The danger of the love of money
keyThemes.explanation:
Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils.

The passage encourages careful attention to attitudes toward money.

keyThemes.theme: Fighting the good fight of faith
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is to flee evil, pursue righteousness and other virtues, and fight the good fight.

Readers are invited to pursue virtue and persevere.

The rich are to do good, be generous, and take hold of that which is truly life.

The chapter encourages generosity as a way to hold wealth rightly.

Timothy is to guard the deposit and avoid irreverent babble and contradictions.

The passage encourages faithfulness to the teaching received.
